Plastic Pollution & Economic Development

A Global Analysis of Corporate Plastic Waste

Author

Alex Pyatigorsky, Brady O’Shea, and Leo Knudsen

Published

May 8, 2026

1 Data Context

This report draws on three complementary datasets to investigate the relationship between corporate plastic waste, national population, and economic development.

1.1 Break Free From Plastic Audit Data

The data were collected and published by Break Free From Plastic, a global movement working to hold corporations accountable for the plastic pollution their products generate. Data were collected across dozens of countries worldwide. Each observation represents a single parent company’s plastic waste recorded in a specific country in a given year, making the country–company–year the observational unit. The dataset covers two annual brand audit cycles: 2019 and 2020. Volunteer teams organized community cleanup events and manually sorted collected plastic items by resin type (HDPE, LDPE, PET, PP, PS, PVC, and “other”), recording the responsible parent company for each piece. The number of volunteers and cleanup events per country are also included. The audit was designed to create transparent, brand-level accountability for plastic pollution and to document which corporations are the largest contributors to the global plastic crisis.

Data cleaning note: The 2019 files contained duplicate polypropylene and polystyrene columns that were combined and removed. The 2020 grand-total column was stored as a character type and converted to numeric. Column names were standardized before merging the two years into one dataset. Three countries were omitted from per-capita visuals: Taiwan, Montenegro, and unlabeled events (“EMPTY”). Taiwan and Montenegro were removed due to implausibly high plastic totals relative to their populations, and unlabeled events could not be attributed to any country.

1.2 U.S. Census Bureau International Database (IDB)

Data were compiled and published by the U.S. Census Bureau as part of its International Programs division. The IDB covers countries and territories worldwide. Each row represents a single country in a single year, making the country–year the observational unit. The extract used here contains demographic estimates for 2019 and 2020, matching the plastic audit years. The Census Bureau derives IDB estimates from a combination of national censuses, vital registration systems, and demographic surveys, applying demographic modeling to fill gaps. Population and land area figures from the IDB allow plastic waste totals to be expressed on a per-capita basis and enable comparisons of waste generation relative to country size.

1.3 World Bank GDP Data

GDP figures were sourced from the World Bank Open Data platform. Coverage is global, with one observation per country per year. GDP values for 2019 and 2020 were extracted to align with the audit years. The World Bank collects national accounts data from member governments and international statistical agencies, reporting both nominal GDP per capita (current USD) and GDP measured at purchasing-power parity (PPP). GDP per capita provides a measure of national wealth, enabling analysis of whether economic development is associated with higher or lower rates of plastic waste generation.

2 Research Questions

2.1 Question 1 — Wealth and Waste

Do wealthier countries produce more plastic waste per capita?

Countries vary enormously in how much plastic waste they generate, but the direction of the relationship with national income is not obvious. High-income countries may produce more consumer packaging, yet they also tend to have more modernized waste-management technology. This question uses the Break Free From Plastic audit data joined with World Bank GDP figures to examine whether GDP per capita predicts per-capita plastic waste across countries.

2.2 Question 2 — Population vs. Economic Output

Is total plastic waste driven more by a country’s population size or its economic output?

Population and GDP per capita are both plausible drivers of plastic waste. A larger population means more consumers, and higher incomes mean more purchasing power and more packaged goods. This question uses the IDB census data merged with the audit and GDP data to investigate these two drivers and assess their relative importance.

3 Data Summaries & Visualizations

3.1 Research Question 1: Wealth and Plastic Waste

3.1.1 Summary Tables

3.1.1.1 Cleanup Activity Statistics

The table below summarizes volunteer participation and cleanup event counts, produced by iterating a custom summary function across both metrics called summarize_variable.

Show Code 
# Custom summary function 
summarize_variable <- function(df, var_name, label) {
  df |>
    rename(.val = all_of(var_name)) |>
    summarise(
      Metric = label,
      Min    = min(.val, na.rm = TRUE),
      Mean   = round(mean(.val, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
      Median = median(.val, na.rm = TRUE),
      SD     = round(sd(.val, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
      IQR    = IQR(.val, na.rm = TRUE),
      Max    = max(.val, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
}

# Iteration across both metrics
map(
  list(
    list(var = "volunteers", label = "Volunteers per Cleanup"),
    list(var = "num_events", label = "Number of Cleanup Events")
  ),
  function(item) summarize_variable(plastics, item$var, item$label)
) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Table 1: Cleanup Activity Summary Statistics",
    subtitle = "Volunteers per cleanup and number of events (2019–2020)"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Metric = "Metric",
    Min    = "Min",
    Mean   = "Mean",
    Median = "Median",
    SD     = "Std. Dev.",
    IQR    = "IQR",
    Max    = "Max"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Min, Mean, Median, SD, IQR, Max),
    decimals = 1,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#2C3E50"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "white"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(80))

3.1.1.2 Proportion of Plastic by Resin Type

Show Code 
# Custom function 
prop_summary <- function(df) {
  df |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols      = c(hdpe, ldpe, o, pet, pp, ps, pvc),
      names_to  = "plastic_type",
      values_to = "count"
    ) |>
    mutate(prop = count / grand_total) |>
    group_by(plastic_type) |>
    summarize(
      mean_prop   = round(mean(prop, na.rm = TRUE), 4),
      total_count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
}

prop_summary(plastics) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Table 2: Plastic Waste by Resin Type",
    subtitle = "Mean proportion and total count across all audits"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    plastic_type = "Plastic Type",
    mean_prop    = "Mean Proportion",
    total_count  = "Total Count"
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns  = mean_prop,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  fmt_integer(
    columns  = total_count,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  text_transform(
    locations = cells_body(columns = plastic_type),
    fn = toupper
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#18BC9C"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "white"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "Summary Statistics",
    columns = c(mean_prop, total_count)
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(70))

3.1.2 Visualizations

3.1.2.1 Top 20 Countries by Total Plastic Waste

Figure 1 shows the twenty countries with the highest total recorded plastic waste, colored by average GDP per capita. High-income countries like the United States and Switzerland appear alongside lower-income nations such as the Philippines and India, suggesting that wealth alone does not determine total waste output. Population scale and data-collection capacity could also be playing a role.

Show Code 
plastics |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(
    total_plastic = sum(grand_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_gdp       = mean(gdp_per_capita_nominal, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(avg_gdp), total_plastic > 0) |>
  slice_max(total_plastic, n = 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_plastic, y = reorder(country, total_plastic), fill = avg_gdp)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(total_plastic)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3, color = "grey30") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::dollar_format()) +
  labs(
    title    = "Top 20 Countries by Total Plastic Waste",
    subtitle = "Colored by average GDP per capita — wealth and waste do not move in lockstep",
    x        = "Total Plastic Waste (piece count)",
    y        = NULL,
    fill     = "GDP per Capita"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position    = "right")

3.1.2.2 Plastic Waste Distribution by GDP Group

Figure 2 compares the distribution of total plastic waste across countries grouped into Low (< $5,000), Middle ($5,000–$20,000), and High (> $20,000) GDP per capita tiers. All three groups show wide, right-skewed distributions. High-GDP countries have a heavier right tail, consistent with greater consumer plastic use, but Low-GDP countries are not far behind which likely reflects a weaker waste-management infrastructure rather than less plastic generation.

Show Code 
plastics |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarize(
    total_plastic      = sum(grand_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_gdp_per_capita = mean(gdp_per_capita_nominal, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(avg_gdp_per_capita)) |>
  mutate(
    gdp_group = ifelse(avg_gdp_per_capita > 20000, "High GDP",
                ifelse(avg_gdp_per_capita <  5000, "Low GDP", "Middle GDP")),
    gdp_group = factor(gdp_group, levels = c("Low GDP", "Middle GDP", "High GDP"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_plastic, y = gdp_group, fill = gdp_group)) +
  geom_density_ridges() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Low GDP"    = "#d5f5ef",
                               "Middle GDP" = "#2C3E50",
                               "High GDP"   = "#fff3cd")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Plastic Waste Distribution by GDP Group",
    subtitle = "Countries grouped by <span style='color: #d5f5ef;'>**Low**</span>, <span style='color: #2C3E50;'>**Middle**</span>, and <span style='color: #fff3cd;'>**High**</span> GDP per Capita",
    x        = "Total Plastic Waste (Log Scale)",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.subtitle   = element_markdown())

3.2.1.2 Mean Plastic Waste, Population, and GDP by GDP Group

The table below is produced by iterating across the three GDP groups and computing group-level summaries for each.

Show Code 
# Iteration across GDP groups 
gdp_groups <- c("Low GDP", "Middle GDP", "High GDP")

country_level <- plastics |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarize(
    total_plastic = sum(grand_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_pop       = mean(population, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_gdp       = mean(gdp_per_capita_nominal, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(avg_gdp)) |>
  mutate(
    gdp_group = ifelse(avg_gdp > 20000, "High GDP",
                ifelse(avg_gdp <  5000, "Low GDP", "Middle GDP")),
    gdp_group = factor(gdp_group, levels = gdp_groups)
  )

map(gdp_groups, function(grp) {
  country_level |>
    filter(gdp_group == grp) |>
    summarise(
      `GDP Group`           = grp,
      `N Countries`         = n(),
      `Mean Total Plastic`  = round(mean(total_plastic, na.rm = TRUE), 0),
      `Mean Population`     = round(mean(avg_pop, na.rm = TRUE), 0),
      `Mean GDP per Capita` = round(mean(avg_gdp, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
    )
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title    = "Table 4: Country-Level Averages by GDP Group",
    subtitle = "Iterative summary across Low, Middle, and High GDP per capita groups"
  ) |>
  fmt_integer(
    columns  = c(`N Countries`, `Mean Total Plastic`, `Mean Population`),
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_currency(
    columns  = `Mean GDP per Capita`,
    currency = "USD",
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#2C3E50"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "white"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#fff3cd"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = `GDP Group` == "High GDP")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#d5f5ef"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = `GDP Group` == "Low GDP")
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "Country Averages",
    columns = c(`Mean Total Plastic`, `Mean Population`, `Mean GDP per Capita`)
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(85))

3.2.2 Visualizations

3.2.2.1 Plastic Waste vs. Population (Log Scale)

Figure 3 shows a strong positive relationship between population and total plastic waste on a log–log scale. Larger countries consistently generate more recorded plastic. The dashed trend line confirms the upward slope, and labeled outliers reveal that some mid-sized countries (e.g., the Philippines) produce disproportionately high totals relative to their population.

Show Code 
scatter_data <- plastics |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(
    total_plastic  = sum(grand_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_population = mean(population, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(avg_population), avg_population > 0, total_plastic > 0)

notable <- scatter_data |>
  arrange(desc(total_plastic)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  bind_rows(scatter_data |> arrange(desc(avg_population)) |> slice_head(n = 5)) |>
  distinct()

ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = avg_population, y = total_plastic)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "grey60", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(color = "dodgerblue", size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = notable, aes(label = country),
                           size = 3.2, color = "grey20",
                           min.segment.length = 0, max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title    = "Plastic Waste Scales with Population Size",
    subtitle = "Log-log scale; dashed line shows linear trend",
    x        = "Population (log scale)",
    y        = "Total Plastic Waste (log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

3.2.2.2 Per-Capita Plastic Waste vs. GDP PPP — Top 10 Countries

Figure 4 juxtaposes the top 10 countries by per-capita plastic waste (left panel) with their respective GDP (PPP) per capita (right panel). The comparison reveals no clear monotonic relationship: Switzerland ranks high on both panels, but several other high-plastic countries have comparatively modest GDPs. This pattern is consistent with the conclusion that population and collection effort — not wealth alone — drive observed waste totals.

4 Data Model

4.1 Model: Total Plastic Waste by Resin Type and Country Area

To formally test whether country size (land area) predicts plastic waste after accounting for resin type, we fit an ordinary least-squares regression of total plastic waste on plastic type and country area (km²). Plastic type is treated as a categorical predictor with HDPE as the reference level.

Show Code 
plastic_types <- c("hdpe", "ldpe", "o", "pet", "pp", "ps", "pvc")

tot_plastic_types <- function(type) {
  plastics |>
    group_by(country) |>
    summarize(
      plastic_type = as.character(type),
      total        = sum(get(type), na.rm = TRUE),
      area         = mean(area.in.square.kilometers, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
}

model_data  <- map(plastic_types, tot_plastic_types) |> bind_rows()
LinearModel <- lm(total ~ plastic_type + area, data = model_data)

tidy(LinearModel) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title    = "Table 5: Linear Model Coefficients",
    subtitle = "Total plastic waste predicted by resin type and country area"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    term      = "Term",
    estimate  = "Estimate",
    std.error = "Std. Error",
    statistic = "t Statistic",
    p.value   = "p-value"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns  = c(estimate, std.error, statistic),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns  = p.value,
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#2C3E50"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "white"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#fff3cd"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = p.value < 0.05)
  ) |>
  tab_footnote(
    footnote  = "Reference category: HDPE. Model R² = 0.034; F(7, 867) = 3.29, p = 0.002. Highlighted rows are statistically significant (p < 0.05)."
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(85))

4.2 Model Interpretation

The linear model regressed total plastic waste on plastic resin type and country land area. Although the model was statistically significant overall (F = 3.29, p = 0.002), it explained very little of the variance in plastic waste (R² = 0.034), indicating that these predictors capture only a small fraction of what drives waste totals.

Using HDPE as the reference category, only the “other” plastic type differed significantly from HDPE — generating approximately 8,578 more units of waste on average (p < 0.05). The remaining resin types (LDPE, PET, PP, PS, PVC) did not differ significantly from HDPE (all p > 0.14).

Critically, country land area was not a significant predictor of total plastic waste (p = 0.738). This finding directly addresses Research Question 2: the physical size of a country does not meaningfully explain how much plastic waste it generates. Combined with the scatter-plot evidence in Figure 3, this points toward population and economic activity — rather than land area — as the primary structural drivers of plastic waste output.
